title: Ancestral Genomes
alt: SUGGESTIONS FOR FUTURE RESEARCH: No further research is needed as it is frankly none of our business.
transcript:
[Cueball and Megan are shown, with Megan using a pointer stick to point at a diagram on a poster. The diagram features tree/root structure with a single node at the top end, branching solid lines leading to more nodes across several levels in most cases, but with at least one node that does not propogate this way and some dotted lines linking down from some branches into other ones. The increasingly branching lower tracks becoming so dense that it almost looks like dark triangles at the bottom of the diagram's last obvious bifurcations. Small and unreadable labels/symbols feature next to most linking lines, and more extensive (but still totally unreadable) information is placed below each of the lowermost 'triangular' terminating clumps.]
Megan: Our admixture analysis showed that these genotypes arose in the ancestral population almost entirely through sexual intercourse.
Megan: Upon realizing this, we of course promptly deleted all our data.
Off-screen voice: What? Why??
Megan: We're not weirdos!
Megan: Jeez, give these people some privacy!
explanation:
A  is the complete genetic makeup of an individual (i.e. all of its genes). In humans, genotypes are almost always inherited from an individual’s parents; the two parents’ genotypes combine during sexual reproduction to form the genotype of the child. Sometimes s do occur, and each human has about 60 such mutations, on average, out of about 20,000 genes. However, most mutations are "silent", not causing any visible changes, and are of minor importance when studying genotypes. That changes in genotype arise through sexual reproduction should not come as any surprise to researchers in the field.

Historically, many societies have had significant taboos around public discussions of sex. While these social norms have shifted significantly over the past century or so, it's still quite common (in the US and other countries), for people to be reluctant to discuss such topics in mixed company. This is particularly true when discussing the sex lives of strangers, which are often seen a very private topic. However, in scientific discussions involving human reproduction sex is commonly discussed — indeed it would be very difficult to study the area without doing so. Generally, such discussions would reduce the taboo by depersonalizing the activity. Furthermore, most of the people involved would be long dead, further reducing any embarrassment there might be about their sexual activity. Megan and Cueball, on the other hand, see the fact their research has 'revealed' sexual activity among the subjects as a major data privacy issue.

Of course, this isn't exclusive to scientific discussion. Any time people have children together, the implication of sex is present, and any time people are married or in a significant romantic relationship, it's often assumed that they're having sex. Public discussions of relationships, marriage, and children are generally seen as unproblematic and neutral topics, but it is generally considered impolite to point out the sexual implications of such discussions. The oddness of this contradiction was a topic of previous strips.

There are genuine privacy issues involved with research into genetic lineage. For example, it may be discovered that a child's legal father is not their biological father, or even that a child is not related to either of their legal parents, and this may be information that people didn't want made public. Researchers often are concerned with the privacy of their research subjects, but this generally takes the form of obscuring personal and identifying data, rather than deleting data altogether. Additionally, when reconstructing genetic lineage, most of the subjects in question are no longer alive, and their information is no longer considered sensitive.

The title text flips the common conclusion of scientific papers that further research is needed. This is because no single study can realistically provide comprehensive data and answer all questions about a topic, so most researchers want to encourage more studies, and may wish to announce their own intention to do further studies. By contrast, here Megan and Cueball are both averse to the idea of future research, because they consider their entire field to be too problematic to pursue. 

Genetics and sex have also appeared in 830: Genetic Analysis. Presenting outlandish or plain bad/incorrect research has been a common topic, such as in 3129: Archaeology Research and 3000: Experimental Astrophysics.
